name: ChapterBridge
card_line: Read or listen to the same book without losing your place.
built_with: Windows, Android, Google Drive, Codex, Claude Code

snapshot.problem: I like switching between reading and listening, depending on whether I’m at my desk or in the car.
snapshot.what_i_built: Lines up an ebook and its audiobook word by word. All three share one saved place.
snapshot.result: On a 22-hour novel, it matched 91% of the words (about 155,000 of 170,000) and flagged the rest for review.

problem: I like switching between reading and listening, depending on whether I’m at my desk or in the car. Every time I switched, I lost my place and ended up scrubbing through hours of audio to find where I left off. The big platforms sync reading and listening, but only for books you buy in their store. Nothing did it for files I already owned, so I built it.

how_it_works.text: Lines up an ebook and its audiobook word by word, using speech-to-text that runs on my own PC.
Lets me read, listen, or follow along with each word highlighted as the narrator reads it. All three share one saved place.
Syncs that place between my PC and phone through my own Google Drive, and works offline on the phone.
Flags passages it couldn’t match instead of guessing.

decisions.decision: My own Google Drive as the backend.
decisions.reason: There’s no server to run, pay for or secure, and the data stays in my account. The app can only see files it created.
The books are copyrighted and private, so I ran Whisper on my PC instead of sending audio to a cloud service. It’s slower, but it’s free and nothing leaves the machine.
Every saved position is kept as history. If my phone and PC disagree, the app asks me which one is right. The farthest point isn’t always where I stopped.
One PC manages the shared library and each phone keeps its own file. For a real product, I’d move to a proper sync service and cloud transcription.
The desktop app only accepts connections from the same computer. Google credentials and the app’s signing key are encrypted with Windows’ built-in protection.

results.label: signed Android releases in about five weeks
automated tests on the desktop side and about 40 Android test suites
lines of Node.js and Java, all written by AI
On a 22-hour novel, it matched 91% of the words (about 155,000 of 170,000) and flagged the rest for review.
